Hatchlings of the Surfbird (Calidris virgata) emerge from eggs incubated at approximately 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a thermal regime that yields an incubation period of 22 days [ab = 22 days], though field records indicate this can range from 21 to 23 days depending on local microclimate conditions. At the moment of hatching, these precocial chicks weigh just 21 grams [Ww0 = 21 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the considerable parental investment required to produce fully developed, downy young capable of thermoregulation and foraging within hours of emergence. This neonatal body mass is broadly consistent with that of other small-bodied migratory shorebirds, although the energetic demands of a high-latitude breeding schedule likely place a premium on rapid early growth. The yolk-dependent embryo undergoes organogenesis within a calcareous egg shell, and the transition to first exogenous feeding occurs promptly after hatching, with the chick's trophic switch marking the onset of independent foraging under the watchful supervision of both parents.

Once the chick embarks on its nestling phase, the developmental trajectory accelerates rapidly toward independence. Under the elevated thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period in this species, approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the young bird achieves sustained flight and fledges after 18 days [tx = 18 days] following hatching, with some broods extending this period to 20 days. This fledging age, relatively short for a charadriiform of this body size, reflects the selective pressures of a brief Arctic or subarctic breeding window, where delays in nest departure could compromise juvenile survival before seasonal resource pulses decline. The fledgling then enters a post-fledging dispersal phase characterized by flight feather maturation and progressive independence from parental provisioning. During this period, the immature bird refines its foraging skills on intertidal invertebrates, gradually building the body condition necessary for migration and eventual reproductive maturation. Nutritional independence onset typically aligns with the completion of skeletal growth, a milestone that precedes the more protracted process of gonadal development.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a distinctly protracted schedule when compared with the rapid pace of fledging. Under the same thermal conditions of 41 °C [T = 41 °C] that define the active metabolic environment, individuals attain puberty at approximately 150 days after hatching [tp = approximately 150 days after hatching], a delay that likely reflects the energetic investment required to complete somatic growth and accumulate sufficient lipid reserves for both migration and the demanding first breeding season. This age at gonadal maturation is notably later than in many other small-bodied scolopacids, possibly due to the species' reliance on a relatively specialized diet of mollusks and crustaceans that necessitates extended learning periods for efficient prey handling. The onset of gametogenesis marks the transition to the sub-adult stage, during which young birds undertake long-distance migrations alongside experienced adults and begin prospecting for future nesting territories. Puberty thus represents a critical life-history bottleneck, as individuals must balance the energetic costs of continued growth, migration, and the initiation of reproductive physiology under the constraints of a short, high-latitude summer.

First breeding is deferred considerably beyond the attainment of sexual maturity, a pattern commonly observed in long-lived migratory shorebirds. The first successful brood typically occurs at 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching], a timing that corresponds to the start of the second potential breeding season for an individual hatched the previous year at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This delay, measured under the same thermal conditions of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], reflects the time needed to establish a territory, secure a mate, and acquire the foraging proficiency required to sustain the energetic costs of egg production and incubation. The species produces exactly one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a reproductive frequency that is low compared to many passerines but typical for a high-latitude shorebird investing heavily in a small number of precocial offspring. Each clutch contains 4 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains 4 eggs], a brood size consistent with other Calidris sandpipers, suggesting a life-history strategy that balances parental investment with a need to maximize annual recruitment within a brief Arctic breeding window.

The maximum recorded lifespan for the Surfbird, documented under field conditions and corroborated by resightings of color-banded individuals, reaches approximately 27.3 years [am = approximately 27.3 years] when measured at the active metabolic temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This exceptional longevity is among the highest recorded for any member of the Calidris genus and is consistent with a slow life-history pace characterized by low annual fecundity and delayed first reproduction. Adult body mass also exhibits clear sexual dimorphism, with females attaining an ultimate wet weight of 216.3 grams [Wwi = 216.3 grams], substantially larger than the male's ultimate wet weight of 186.9 grams [Wwi = 186.9 grams]. This pronounced size difference likely reflects the energetic demands of egg production in the female, despite the single-egg clutch, as well as potential roles in resource partitioning and mate competition. The combination of extreme longevity, low reproductive output, and marked sexual size dimorphism positions the Surfbird as an outlier among its congeners, illustrating how life-history evolution in a specialized intertidal niche can produce demographic strategies that diverge sharply from shorebird norms.
